q: The earliest expression of the computational view of thought, per Haugeland, is Hobbes':
a: 'Reasoning is but reckoning'
e: It took three centuries, until electronic computers, for the idea to catch on.

q: For Haugeland, what makes a project count as AI isn't protoplasm vs. semiconductor, but whether:
a: The product is designed and specified in terms of a computational structure
e: A DuPont synthetic-organic android probably wouldn't count. An IBM programmed robot probably would.

q: Which three dilemmas does Haugeland say the computational idea 'slices through at a stroke'?
a: Mind/matter interaction, explaining meaning without a homunculus, and the testability of mentalistic explanation
e: Cognitive scientists can be materialists AND mentalists, explaining by rules without an unexplained homunculus.

q: Why does Haugeland say there can't be a dynamics of thought like physical dynamics?
a: Particles obey laws infallibly, but people must work to follow rules of reason, which seems to require an understanding rule-applier
w: Thoughts are too small to measure
e: That rule-applier looks like a homunculus 'directing thoughts like a traffic cop', which begs the question.

q: Haugeland says the chess-playing machine is philosophically inspiring because:
a: Its decisions cause physical behavior without violating physics or needing an unexplained 'compunculus'
e: It follows rules of the game and rules of thumb, and there's a determinate answer about what reasoning it went through.

q: Haugeland defines a computer as:
a: An automatic formal system
e: A formal system is like a game where tokens are manipulated according to rules.

q: To define a formal system you specify three things:
a: What the tokens are, the starting position, and what moves are allowed
e: Example: peg-jumping solitaire, where the goal is one peg left in the center.

q: A formal system is 'digital' because it is:
a: Self-contained, perfectly definite, and finitely checkable
e: The weather or the state of the economy make no difference to the game. There are no borderline cases.

q: The domino triad-switching game turns out to be 'essentially the same' as peg-jumping. This illustrates:
a: Formal equivalence
e: Positions correspond one-to-one, starting positions correspond, and legal moves correspond.

q: In fancy chess sets, every pawn figurine is different, but they're all the same TYPE because:
a: The rules treat them identically: tokens of the same type are formally interchangeable
w: They're made of the same material
They start on the same row
e: Type is fixed by how the rules treat a token, not by its appearance.

q: How can the algebra game have finitely checkable moves despite indefinitely many formula types?
a: Formulas are built from a small set of atomic tokens, and rules apply by structure
w: Only a few formulas are allowed
e: Positions of one system (the well-formed-formula game) serve as tokens of a higher-level system.

q: Combining Church's thesis and Turing's theorem gives the result that a universal Turing machine can:
a: Imitate any automatic formal system whatsoever (given programming)
e: Real computers are universal machines, except that their storage is limited.

q: When a Turing machine imitates another system, the part that corresponds directly to the imitated system is the ______, and the behind-the-scenes part is the ______.
a: Virtual machine; program
e: Languages like BASIC, FORTRAN, LISP are really convenient universal machines imitated by hardware.

q: Why does Haugeland say it's foolish to call computers 'nothing but number crunchers'?
a: A physical object can be many machines at once, and the level that matters may have nothing to do with bits
e: A particular object is a particular machine only at a particular level of description.

q: The 'control problem' in automating a formal system is:
a: How the device selects which move to make when several are legal
w: How to get the device to obey the rules
e: In chess, listing legal moves is easy. Choosing among them is the difference between amateurs and world champions.

q: Looking ahead 40 moves in chess would involve about 10¹²⁰ possibilities. This is called:
a: Combinatorial explosion
e: Fewer than 10¹⁸ seconds have passed since the universe began. The solution is to consider only relevant moves.

q: An algorithm is guaranteed to give a result meeting certain conditions. A heuristic is:
a: A more-or-less reliable rule of thumb that isn't infallible
e: 'Never trade your queen for a pawn' is a heuristic for winning. A machine can infallibly follow fallible rules.

q: A multi-position selector switch vs. a continuous tuning dial illustrates:
a: Digital vs. analog
e: You can't set a switch between AM and FM, but a dial can sit between stations.

q: What's the 'overwhelming advantage' of poker chips over tablespoons of colored sand?
a: All bets are exact: digital tokens eliminate measurement error that propagates
e: With ±2% sand error, betting 613 is pointless (the white units drop out). With chips, 613 is easy.

q: Why does Haugeland call 'any analog device can be digitally simulated' grossly misleading?
a: Simulation needs a compact, precise description of the relevant relationships, which systems like drugged lab rats lack
e: 'In principle, rats are made of atoms' is 'utterly out to lunch'.

q: Formal tokens can lead 'two lives'. They are:
a: Syntactical (meaningless markers moved by rules) and semantic (having meanings related to the world)
e: How the two lives get together is the foundation of modern logic and the inspiration of cognitive science.

q: Given true axioms and truth-preserving rules, 'if you take care of the syntax, ______.'
a: The semantics will take care of itself
w: The hardware will take care of itself
The homunculus will take care of it
e: So proving a theorem formally establishes its semantic truth.

q: An automatic formal system with an interpretation such that the semantics takes care of itself is what Dennett calls a:
a: Semantic engine
e: The discovery that semantic engines are possible is the basic inspiration of cognitive science and AI.

q: The 'arithmetic salad' example shows that, among trillions of interpretations of the same tokens, we prefer the one that:
a: Makes the outputs come out true (and sensible)
w: Is the simplest to write down
Makes the outputs look like equations
e: The tokens themselves never favor one interpretation. Truth is what makes one 'righter'.

q: 'GOFAI' stands for:
a: Good Old-Fashioned AI
e: Also called classical, symbol-manipulation, or language-of-thought AI. It dominated from the mid-50s through the mid-80s.

q: Symbols differ from chess pieces in that:
a: Symbols mean something; chess pieces are merely formal game tokens
w: Symbols are physical, chess pieces are not
Chess pieces are digital, symbols aren't
e: Numerals represent numbers. Chess pieces, checkers and go stones represent nothing.

q: Haugeland says all interpretation, including translation, is:
a: Holistic: you can't interpret a brief string completely out of context
e: A single string might come out true on two schemes by coincidence. Only a consistent pattern across many cases matters.

q: For a system's intermediate token strings to count as genuine reasoning steps, it must:
a: Handle an open-ended range of problems AND actually arrive at solutions through those steps
e: Otherwise it's 'a kind of fraud', e.g., solving another way and tacking on fake 'steps'.

q: Early GOFAI systems were clever on carefully posed problems but prone to amusing blunders because they lacked:
a: Common sense
e: Later work shifted to large-scale knowledge representation, where the biggest problem was organization.

q: Which is NOT one of the disappointments of GOFAI Haugeland lists?
a: Inability to perform explicit reasoning
e: Explicit reasoning is GOFAI's strength. Its weaknesses led some to explore 'new-fangled AI' (NFAI).

q: Connectionist networks differ from GOFAI in having:
a: Many simple interconnected units with no central processor and no separate memory store
e: Connectionism is the most prominent 'NFAI' approach. It addresses GOFAI's weaknesses but isn't yet good at its strengths.
